name: The Cedar of Lebanon in Victoria Square
access: Free. Victoria Square garden is now a council-maintained public park (it was a keyholders' garden until the wartime removal of its railings). No opening hours found; the garden is open to walk through.
transport: Central Clifton, about 1.6 km (20 min walk) west of Queen Square; about 10 min walk up from College Green / Park Street. Computed from coordinates, no stop checked.
verify_notes: Source A, Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey (Richard Bland, ST 5728 7313, which converts to 51.45553,-2.61623, inside the square): girth 595 cm, 'age 150 years', 'one of the few trees from the original planting', horizontal branches about 20 m long. BTF's age is its own estimate, so the range here is broad (BTF says 150; the Clifton and Hotwells society dates the square's first planting to about 1840, and another source gives about 1860; no source says this tree belongs to a dated planting, so no bridge made). Source B, Clifton and Hotwells Improvement Society's communal-gardens guide: Victoria Square (ca. 1840) is now a public park, the Council maintains it, and a fine Lebanon cedar is among the surviving original plantings; a 2015 clearance and replanting is recorded. Source C, Dick Isles memoir (same society): a large stone urn once stood under the cedar of Lebanon; before the war the gardens had four locked gates and residents held keys; wartime railing removal left them open to all. Alive: lifecheck.py 51.4562 -2.6163 returned RECENT 2026-05-17 (iNaturalist, generic nearby observation, not proof for this trunk); the square was replanted 2015 and the cedar is described as surviving. Same spot, other trees to fold into the page as context only: Fern-leaved Beech (BTF, girth 480 cm, original planting c1860, ST5727 7310), an old horizontal Black Mulberry, an Italian Maple (girth 280 cm), and a chimera hornbeam; none is a separate collectible point. Pin is the BTF grid reference (10 m resolution, judged unreliable by an earlier pass), so approximate; the square is small and the cedar is the dominant tree. Hard-rule check: this is not one of the private Clifton garden squares the earlier pass left out; the Clifton society and council sources say Victoria Square specifically is now public. Single-species survey plus two local-society pages; not a register.

name: The Harbour Wall Fig

location.address: Floating Harbour wall east of Bristol Bridge, Castle Park, Bristol BS1

access: Free. Seen from the Castle Park path along the Floating Harbour, open at all times (Bristol City Council: no charge, open at all times). The tree grows out of the harbour wall itself, so it is viewed, not touched.
transport: Beside Bristol Bridge, about 0.55 km (7 min walk) from Queen Square and about 1 km (13 min) from Temple Meads. Computed from coordinates, no stop checked.
verify_notes: Source A, Bristol Tree Forum (ST 5910 7303, converts to 51.45476,-2.59002): a huge fig in the thirty-foot vertical wall of Bristol Docks just east of Bristol Bridge; the wall was part of the old castle's defences; how it got established and how long ago is a mystery; 'every so often it is heavily reduced so that it does not create problems for the river traffic'. Source B, Avon Stories (a Bristol river blogger, Sept 2018): at least two figs in Castle Park; the huge one opposite the old brewery is thought the oldest, visible in historic photographs from 1905 (Know Your Place), the 1920s, 1930 and 1951; figs along the Avon, harbour and Malago were seeded by accident from trade (fruit from boats, ballast). A storm on 31 July 2018 pulled half of it out of the wall and the Harbour Master team removed the debris from the water. Alive now: two iNaturalist observations of Ficus carica with GPS accuracy 3 to 4 m at 51.45485,-2.58990 (2026-07-23, research grade; 2026-10-14), which is within about 10 m of the BTF grid reference; confirmed pin on that evidence (a GPS fix at the tree). Caveat for the writer: after the 2018 storm the tree is a regrown, reduced fig, not the full mass that stood in 1905; whether the two sources' 'huge' fig is exactly this plant is inferred from the position, not stated. Age: no source dates this specimen; 'over a century' rests only on the blogger saying the fig is visible in 1905 photographs, so state that as the blogger's claim. No girth (a wall tree). Lead, not delivered: the second sprawling fig on the New Cut bank by the Bath Bridge roundabout (BTF, ST 5961 7215, no GPS or recent observation found).

name: The Brandon Hill Oak

location.address: Brandon Hill, Bristol BS1 5RR (near the park-keepers' compound)

access: Free. Brandon Hill is a council public park. BTF places the tree 'just inside the park-keepers compound', so it may stand behind a depot fence: view it from the park paths; I could not check the fence line. No pin on a viewing place beyond the grid reference.
transport: Right by College Green / Park Street, about 1 km (13 min walk) west of Queen Square. Computed from coordinates, no stop checked.
verify_notes: FLAGGED, single source for the tree itself. Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey (ST 5781 7291, converts to 51.45359,-2.60857): Common Oak, girth 500 cm, 'age 300' (BTF's estimate), 'magnificent tree with boughs twenty metres long', 'just inside the park-keepers compound but dominates the area', 'the oldest tree in this extraordinary park, which has been a public open space for 800 years' (the 800 years is BTF's phrase; the council and Parks and Gardens UK page confirm Brandon Hill is a public park, the council page lists a tree trail by the Friends of Brandon Hill, which I could not read as it is a compressed PDF). Alive: lifecheck.py returned RECENT 2024-12-01 (iNaturalist, generic nearby observation); no observation of a large oak at this exact point found, three oak observations lie 80 to 120 m away. Access question to settle on the ground: whether the oak is visible from outside the compound. Walking cluster note: the Wellingtonia (girth 300 cm, planted 1973, BTF ST5787 7286) and the Keaki, Swedish whitebeam and Pride of India on this hill are young or small and were not delivered.

name: The Royal Fort Black Mulberry

location.address: Royal Fort Gardens, Tyndall Avenue, Bristol BS8 1UH

access: Free. The University of Bristol says Royal Fort Gardens are open daily all year to the public with no ticket (its other gardens are by invitation or tour). Opening hours not fetched.
transport: Below Tyndall Avenue and the Wills Memorial Building, about 0.9 km (12 min walk) north-west of Queen Square, a few minutes up Park Street from College Green. Computed from coordinates, no stop checked.
verify_notes: FLAGGED: one survey plus GPS observations; no age. Bristol Tree Forum (ST 5833 7331, converts to 51.45722,-2.60114): 'the largest' Black Mulberry in the city, in the gardens of the Royal Fort, girth 230 cm; mulberries are often found growing horizontally. A Garden News UK column (2021) calls an old, bent mulberry its favourite thing in the gardens (read as a search snippet only; not used for a figure). Pin: three iNaturalist observations of Morus nigra at Royal Fort Gardens (2019-04-26, 2019-04-27, 2025-07-22, GPS accuracy 4 to 8 m, research grade for two) sit at 51.45723 to 51.45727,-2.60116 to -2.60126, within about 7 m of the BTF grid reference, so the tree is placed and confirmed; the 2025 observation also shows it alive. A mulberry register entry (2007) puts one 'near the east exit by the engineering building overhanging a path', a coarse hint only. Royal Fort Gardens is a walk-through garden, not a small site, so no location_site. BTF also names a young Dawyck beech, Italian cypress, Kapuka and young Yellow Buckeye in the same garden, and a Persian Ironwood by the Wills Tower (ST5815 7318); all minor, not delivered. No sentence available that dates the mulberry; if the writer wants to say it is old, only the 230 cm girth and the leaning habit are sourced.

name: The Mina Road Park Plane

location.address: Mina Road Park, St Werburghs, Bristol BS2 9YG

access: Free. Mina Road Park is a council park, listed as open all year (Wikipedia, Bristol City Council as operator). Hours not found.
transport: St Werburghs, about 2.6 km (35 min walk) north-east of Queen Square, near Stapleton Road and Montpelier stations (distance computed; no stop checked).
verify_notes: FLAGGED, single source for the tree. Bristol Tree Forum (ST 6014 7443, converts to 51.46743,-2.57521): the group of plane trees in Mina Road Park are 'stunning' and 'all the same age, having been planted c 1880'; this one is the largest, girth 620 cm (the 13th largest tree in BTF's over-5-metre list). Age is BTF's planting date, so about 140 years, not independently checked: Wikipedia says the park was laid out by Frederick Ashmead and opened 30 June 1886 with a Victorian planting scheme of Wellingtonia, deodar and Cryptomeria, and that the present-day park has an older group of London planes alongside acacia and Norway maples but gives no ages; Parks and Gardens UK says the ground was given to the Corporation in 1884. So a c1880 planting predating the 1886 opening is plausible but unconfirmed. Alive: lifecheck returned RECENT 2024-02-12 (iNaturalist, generic nearby observation, no plane-specific record). The 620 cm girth is large for a plane of that age; a writer should state it as BTF's measurement. Outside the walkable centre cluster (about 2.6 km from Queen Square). Cluster note: the BTF entry says all the planes are the same age, so which trunk is the 620 cm one cannot be told from sources.

name: The Saville Road Horse Chestnut

location.address: Saville Road, Durdham Down (the Downs), Bristol BS9

access: Free. The Downs are public open common managed by the Downs Committee; the tree stands beside Saville Road on the Downs edge. Open at all times.
transport: About 3.2 km (40 min walk) north of Queen Square on the edge of Durdham Down; the Downs are served by city buses (no stop checked).

name: The Parish Yew, Leigh Woods

location.address: Parish wall, Leigh Woods National Nature Reserve, near the National Trust reserve office, Valley Road, Bristol BS8 3PL

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Leigh Woods (1)

access: Free. Leigh Woods is open woodland run by the National Trust; the veteran tree walk (1 mile, 30 to 45 minutes, easy) starts at the North Road entrance, grid ref ST555730; roadside parking on North Road.
transport: Bus 357, 358 or 359 along the A369, nearest stop about 100 m from North Road, then about 10 minutes on foot to the tree. Clifton Down station 2.6 km.

location_site.name: Parish wall by the NT reserve office, Leigh Woods

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk bulging around the stones of the old parish wall, with stretches of wall removed either side and woodchip over the roots. It stands beside the surfaced path near the reserve office.
story:
This yew is slowly eating a wall. It grows in a gap in the old stone parish boundary that runs through Leigh Woods, and its trunk has bulged out around the stones and swallowed part of them. The National Trust, which looks after the woods, eventually stopped arguing with it. It took away short stretches of wall on either side to give the tree room, and laid woodchip around its roots.

The Trust puts it at approximately 500 years old and calls it one of the oldest trees in Leigh Woods. That is the Trust's estimate rather than a ring count. The Ancient Yew Group, which keeps a database of Britain's old yews, measured the trunk at 4.6 metres round in 2004 and classes it as ancient, without offering an age of its own.

It is also what foresters call a maiden tree. Many old trees in working woods were pollarded or coppiced, cut back so they would regrow as a crop of poles. The Trust says this one never was. Whatever happened to the wood around it, the yew has been left to grow in its own shape for its whole life.

A parish wall is built to mark a line for good. Here the wall is the thing that had to give way. The tree is stage 2 of the Trust's veteran tree walk, about ten minutes from the North Road entrance.

name: The Nightingale Valley Plane

location.address: Nightingale Valley, beside Brislington Brook and its weir, Brislington, Bristol

access: Free. Public woodland path along Brislington Brook (Nightingale Valley); the trunk can be seen from the path by the weir. Paths can be muddy; no hours.
transport: Bristol Temple Meads about 4 km; nearest rail stop St Anne's Park about 600 m north-west by the brook path (computed from coordinates, not checked on a timetable).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bricked-up opening in its vast hollow trunk, 6.75 metres round. It stands beside the weir on Brislington Brook in Nightingale Valley, seen from the woodland path.
story:
Somebody bricked this tree up. The London plane beside the weir in Nightingale Valley is hollow, and people had taken to lighting fires inside it, so the open trunk was filled in with brickwork to stop them. It worked. The plane is still alive, and the brick patch has become the easiest way to tell it from everything else along Brislington Brook.

It is a big tree to have survived that. The Bristol Tree Forum measured the trunk at 6.75 metres round, says the crown fills the little valley of the brook, and estimates it at about 250 years old. That age is the Forum's own estimate from the size, not a planting date. The Forum also thinks the tree was probably associated with nearby Brislington House, though it gives no record of who planted it or when.

A walker who wrote up the brook path in 2018 passed on the local view that this is the oldest plane in Bristol. Nobody has published the measurements to settle it, so take that as what people round here say rather than a fact we can stand behind. It would not be a surprising title. The other big planes the city is known for, in Queen Square and Mina Road Park, were planted around the 1880s.

The brook path can be muddy after rain. The whole trunk can be seen from the path by the weir, with no need to leave it.

name: The Monterey Cypress at Bishops Knoll

location.address: Bishops Knoll Wood, Bramble Lane, Stoke Bishop, Bristol BS9 1JH

access: Free. Woodland Trust wood, open access; main entrance on Bramble Lane (public road with pavement, wide gate). A public footpath crosses the site; some uneven steps. No car park, a few spaces on Bramble Lane.
transport: Nearest bus stop Julian Road, 1 km walk on pavement (Woodland Trust).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the Victorian iron railings still standing round its trunk, which is over seven metres in girth. It stands inside Bishops Knoll Wood, among the old grounds of the demolished Knoll mansion.
story:
The house whose garden this cypress grew up in has been gone for half a century, and its railings have not. Bishops Knoll Wood was once the grounds of The Knoll, a mansion built in the late 19th century for Peter Prankerd and demolished in the 1970s. The Monterey cypress still stands inside the Victorian ironwork that was put round it, a fence guarding a garden that no longer exists.

It has grown into what the Bristol Tree Forum calls a colossal specimen. The Forum measured the trunk at 7.1 metres round, and the Woodland Trust, which now owns the wood, gives it a girth of over seven metres.

The Forum's age is a piece of reasoning rather than a record. Monterey cypress reached Britain in 1839, and the Forum argues this one cannot have gone in earlier than 1860, which puts it somewhere around 150 to 170 years old. Nobody has a planting date.

The species has a second claim on British gardens. The Forum points out that Monterey cypress is one parent of the Leyland cypress, the fast-growing conifer behind so many garden hedges. This is what one side of that family looks like when it is left alone for a century and a half.

The wood is free to walk into from Bramble Lane. A giant coast redwood and a vast Austrian black pine stand in the same old grounds.

name: The Bundle-planted Sessile Oak, Bishops Knoll

location.address: Bishops Knoll Wood, Bramble Lane entrance, Stoke Bishop, Bristol BS9 1JH

access: Free. Woodland Trust wood, open access, entrance on Bramble Lane; the oak is the first big tree on entering (Woodland Trust).
transport: Nearest bus stop Julian Road, 1 km walk on pavement (Woodland Trust).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the several fused stems that make one broad trunk, seven metres round. It stands close to the Bramble Lane entrance among apple and other fruit trees, partly screened by young ash.
story:
This oak may be six trees pretending to be one. The Woodland Trust thinks it was planted as a bundle, six or so young oaks set in a single hole, which over the centuries fused into one trunk. That would explain why it is so portly, seven metres round. The Bristol Tree Forum agrees it may have been a bundle planting, noting that its several stems do not appear to grow from an old pollard cut, the other usual reason an oak ends up with many trunks.

How old it is depends on whom you ask. The Woodland Trust, which owns the wood, says it could be as much as 600 years old and probably dates from the medieval deer park that once covered this ground. The Forum puts it at 700. Both are estimates from the size of a tree whose size may be the work of six. Either way it was growing here centuries before The Knoll, the Victorian mansion whose grounds became this wood, and long before the Monterey cypress a short walk away.

The two sources also disagree on how easy it is to spot. The Trust describes it looming through apple and other fruit trees as the first thing to catch the eye when you come in from Bramble Lane. The Forum says it is disguised by young ash trees and not easy to find. Look near the entrance, among the fruit trees, for a broad oak made of several fused stems.

name: The Blaise Meadow Sweet Chestnut

location.address: Meadow off Henbury Road, Blaise Castle Estate, Henbury, Bristol BS10 7QS

access: Free. Blaise Castle Estate is a council-owned public park (Wikipedia); meadow off Henbury Road. No opening hours found.
transport: Bus to Henbury / Blaise Castle area; not checked. About 7 km north-west of the centre (computed).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the vast horizontal limbs spreading from a trunk seven metres round. It stands in the meadow off Henbury Road on the Blaise Castle Estate, beside a sycamore that grows on five trunks.
story:
If the Bristol Tree Forum's estimate is right, this chestnut was already around 300 years old when Humphry Repton came to Blaise to design the parkland. The Forum puts it at about 550 years, with a trunk seven metres round, and describes its vast horizontal branches reaching out across the meadow off Henbury Road.

That age is the Forum's own figure, worked out from a tree nobody has dated, and we have found no second written source for this particular chestnut. A girth of seven metres is in keeping with a sweet chestnut several centuries old, but treat 550 as an estimate. On the Forum's figure it would have been growing here through the late medieval centuries, the Civil War, and the years after 1789, when the banker John Scandrett Harford bought the estate and had Repton reshape the grounds into the Picturesque park that is now free for anyone to walk.

The chestnut does not have the meadow to itself, and its neighbours are part of the reason to come. The Forum lists a sycamore beside it that grows on five trunks, each about 2.8 metres round and seven metres around all together, and the stump of an old common lime that has rotted down and thrown up a thicket of thin new trunks from its base. Three trees in one field, each refusing to grow the way a tree in a textbook does.

If you know more about its history, tell us.

name: The Wellingtonias by the Lower Pond, Combe Dingle

location.address: Combe Dingle, by the lower pond on the Trym, Blaise Castle Estate, Bristol BS10

access: Free. Within the public Blaise Castle Estate (council-owned, Wikipedia); on the slope beside the stream near the lower pond.
transport: Not checked; Coombe Dingle suburb adjoins the estate. About 6.5 km north-west of the centre (computed).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as two very tall giant sequoias standing together, the thicker one, 7.1 metres round, on the stream side. They stand on the slope beside the stream near the lower pond in Combe Dingle.
story:
Two Californian giants stand thirty metres apart at the bottom of a Bristol valley, beside a stream and a small pond. The thicker of the pair measures 7.1 metres round, which makes it, according to the Bristol Tree Forum, the largest of the three Wellingtonias on the Blaise Castle Estate. Its partner, about 30 metres away, is 6 metres round.

Wellingtonia is the British name for the giant sequoia, the species of the biggest trees on Earth in the Sierra Nevada, and in Britain it is a newcomer. The Forum's account is that seed reached the Veitch nursery in 1855. It dates the smaller of these two at about 150 years. That is an estimate from the species' arrival, not a planting record, so the pair are best thought of as somewhere between 150 and 170 years old.

That makes them young by the standards of this list, and by the standards of their own species, which can live for thousands of years in California. Here, beside the lower pond on the Trym, they are a century and a half into that. The third of the estate's Wellingtonias, 33 metres tall, stands near the house, about 900 metres away.

We have only the Forum's survey for these trees. If you know more about who planted them, tell us.

name: The Oldbury Court Sweet Chestnut

location.address: Oldbury Court Estate, Fishponds, Bristol BS16

access: Free. Oldbury Court Estate is a public park beside the River Frome (Wikipedia).
transport: Fishponds, about 4.8 km north-east of the centre (Wikipedia); bus not checked.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing alone in the middle of a wide grassy area, a clean trunk 5.9 metres round under a broad head of branches. It stands in the open centre of Oldbury Court Estate.
story:
One tree runs this park. The Bristol Tree Forum says this sweet chestnut dominates Oldbury Court, a massive veteran standing on its own in the middle of a wide stretch of grass, with a clean trunk 5.9 metres round and a fine head of branches above it. In a park of big trees, it is the one you see first.

The Forum estimates it at about 400 years old. That is the Forum's figure, from a tree that has never been dated, and we have only its survey for this particular chestnut, so take the number as a careful guess rather than a record. On that estimate it would have been growing here since the early 1600s, long before Oldbury Court became a public park in Fishponds and before Humphry Repton, the landscape designer, was brought in to advise on the grounds.

Sweet chestnuts are not native to Britain. Nobody has left a record of how this one came to stand here. Its neighbours give a sense of the place. The Forum also lists two big oaks on the northern edge of the estate, above the gorge of the River Frome, at around 380 years old.

If you know its history, tell us.

name: The Hermitage Wood Horse Chestnuts, Stoke Park

location.address: Hermitage Wood, Stoke Park, Stoke Gifford / Bristol BS16

access: Free. Hermitage Wood lies in Stoke Park, a public park; BTF does not state hours. Access not independently checked.
transport: Not checked; Stoke Park is about 5 km north-east of the centre (computed).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the biggest of three old horse chestnuts, 5.5 metres round, the largest trees in Hermitage Wood. It stands on the eastern edge of the wood in Stoke Park.
story:
The biggest trees in Hermitage Wood are not the native oaks or ash you might expect, but three horse chestnuts, a species from the Balkans. The Bristol Tree Forum records all three as veterans. The largest, on the eastern edge of the wood, is 5.5 metres round. The other two, 5.05 and 5 metres, stand in a corner of the wood and on the northern edge of the main path, all within about 300 metres of each other.

The Forum thinks they were probably planted for aesthetic reasons, and that they are probably about 300 years old. That age is the Forum's guess, and we could not find a second source to confirm it. If it holds, they would be old for their kind, a species that only reached Britain in the 17th century.

The wood sits inside Stoke Park, a public park on the north-eastern edge of Bristol. Nobody has published who planted them, or exactly when.

They are at their best in May, when the big leaves are fresh and the trees carry their upright spikes of white flowers, and again in autumn when the conkers come down. If you know more about the trio, tell us.

best_time.label: May, when all three chestnuts carry their upright spikes of white flowers

name: The Kings Weston Deodar

location.address: Beside Kings Weston House, Kings Weston Lane, Bristol BS11 0UT

access: Free to see from the parkland around the house (the Kings Weston estate parkland is open; the house itself is a conference and wedding venue). Opening hours not stated.
transport: Not checked; Kings Weston is about 7 km north-west of the centre (computed).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge limb that leaves the trunk almost at ground level and runs out sideways. It stands beside Kings Weston House, a deodar cedar 4.3 metres round.
story:
Most cedars hold their great limbs well above your head. This one throws a huge branch out sideways almost at ground level, from so low on the trunk that the limb starts where most trees are still all trunk. The Bristol Tree Forum picked it as one of twenty remarkable Bristol trees that hold no national record, and that branch is the reason.

The tree is a deodar, the Himalayan cedar, with a trunk 4.3 metres round, and it grows right beside Kings Weston House. Sir John Vanbrugh designed it for Edward Southwell in the early 18th century, and it was remodelled between 1845 and 1850. Whether the cedar is as old as that remodelling, no source we have found says, and the Forum gives no age. So it stays undated here, and if you know when it was planted, tell us.

The parkland around the house is open to walk through, and the cedar can be seen from it. The house itself is a wedding and conference venue rather than a museum. The Oak of Kings Weston, older than Vanbrugh's house, stands in the same estate and makes the pair worth one walk.

name: The Snuff Mills Quarry-edge Oak

location.address: Edge of the former quarry cliff, Snuff Mills park, Frome Valley, Bristol BS16

access: Free. Snuff Mills is a public riverside park on the Frome (Wikipedia). The tree is on the edge of the path above the quarry cliff, and seen from the lower path in winter.
transport: Not checked; Stapleton, about 5 km north-east of the centre (computed).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its position, a squat old oak right on the lip of the old quarry cliff at the edge of the upper path. In winter it shows from the lower path by the river.
story:
This oak grows on the lip of a sheer drop. Snuff Mills was quarried once, and the old quarry face along the Frome valley is now a vertical cliff. The oak stands right at its top edge, beside the path, with nothing much between its roots and the air. The Bristol Tree Forum, which put it on its list of twenty remarkable Bristol trees that hold no national record, says simply that it defies gravity.

The Forum calls it very ancient and squat, which is about all anyone has written down. There is no published girth and no age, not even a rough estimate, and we have found no second source for this particular tree. If you know how old it is, or have measured it, tell us.

What the Forum does say is where to look. In summer the oak is one tree among many along the top path. In winter, with the leaves down, it shows from the lower path along the river, a low, broad shape hunched on the very edge of the cliff above you. That is the view worth coming for, and it needs no scrambling.

Snuff Mills is a public riverside park on the Frome in Stapleton, free and open to walk. A small-leaved lime with weeping branches grows on the riverbank a few hundred metres along the river, listed by the same survey.

best_time.label: winter, when the bare oak shows from the lower path, hunched on the edge of the quarry cliff
